title: Vortex anisotropy in chiral and nematic superconductors with strain
abstract: Unconventional superconductors with a two-component order parameter support the existence of a rotational symmetry breaking nematic phase and a time-reversal symmetry breaking chiral phase. A recent experiment on 4Hb-TaS$_2$ surprisingly shows both twofold anisotropy in $H_{c2}$, which suggests nematic superconductivity, as well as isotropic vortices at low temperatures, which suggest chiral superconductivity. To resolve this apparent conundrum we write down the appropriate Ginzburg-Landau equations and develop a numerically efficient algorithm for finding vortex solutions, allowing us to study their shape and anisotropy over a broad parameter range. We also demonstrate analytically that, to leading order, the vortex anisotropy is independent of strain in the nematic case, but is linearly dependent on it in the chiral phase, providing a possible way to distinguish the two phases. Using all these results we show that, in the presence of strain, in a large parameter regime the system behaves nematically near the transition, leading to an anisotropy of $H_{c2}$, but is dominantly chiral away from the transition, leading to parametrically smaller vortex anisotropy, in line with the experiment.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes vortex anisotropy in superconductors exhibiting nematic or chiral symmetry breaking, using a Ginzburg-Landau framework. By developing numerical and analytical solutions, the authors show that the strain dependence of the vortex anisotropy differs significantly between the two phases. This provides a robust theoretical tool to help experimentally distinguish between nematic and chiral superconducting states.
main_problem: The paper investigates the vortex anisotropy in unconventional superconductors that exhibit both nematic and chiral superconducting phases, specifically examining how uniaxial strain affects this anisotropy.
main_result: The vortex anisotropy exhibits distinct functional dependencies on strain for the nematic versus the quasi-chiral phase, providing a potential experimental diagnostic to distinguish between these two superconducting states.
method: The study employs a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau approach, utilizing numerical simulations (TDGL) and analytical perturbation theory to solve for vortex solutions.
model_or_system: The system models unconventional superconductors with a two-component order parameter, governed by a free energy functional that includes terms for nematicity and chirality, and is perturbed by uniaxial strain.
key_observables: Vortex shape and anisotropy ($A_B$), critical magnetic field anisotropy ($A_{H_{c2}}$), and the nematicity parameter.
important_parameters: Uniaxial strain ($\epsilon$), deviation from critical temperature ($\alpha$), and phenomenological parameters ($F_4$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a phenomenological Ginzburg-Landau free energy expansion and uses approximations (e.g., Fourier series expansion, perturbative expansion) to solve the coupled differential equations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing coexistence of Normal, Nematic, and Quasi-chiral phases, and plot the evolution of vortex anisotropy ($A_B$) versus temperature/strain, demonstrating different scaling behaviors for the two phases.
paper_structure: The paper develops the Ginzburg-Landau equations, applies numerical methods (TDGL) and analytical techniques (perturbation theory in Fourier space) to solve for vortex solutions, and compares the resulting anisotropy scaling laws for the nematic and quasi-chiral regimes.
why_interesting: The detailed study of symmetry breaking and phase transitions in superconducting order parameters, particularly the coupling between strain and superconducting symmetry, is highly relevant to understanding exotic quantum states in condensed matter systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Phase diagram for a homogeneous two-component superconductor. The different colours of shaded regions indi- cate the different phases, with green, blue and red standing for normal, nematic, and quasi-chiral phases, respectively. The slope of the borderline between the normal and nematic phase is always ±1. (a) For β > 0, only the normal and nematic phases are allowed. (b) For β < 0, the quasi-chiral phase is also allowed. The slope of the borderline between the nematic and quasi-chiral phase is ± β 1+β .

FIG. 2. Nematicity of a homogeneous two-component super- conductor with β < 0 as a function of α for ϵ = 0.05. An initially quasi-chiral state becomes nematic at a transition point given by Eq. (7), after which it is in the nematic phase until α = |ϵ|.

FIG. 3. The solution for the magnetic field B(r) of a single vortex core with parameters α = −1, F2 = 0, F4 = 0.1, ϵ = −0.05 in two different phases: (a) Nematic phase with β = 0.1 and (b) Quasi-chiral phase with β = −0.1. In the inset plots, the x- and y-axis profiles of the magnetic field are shown, as well as a red line showing the half-maximal magnetic field level, Bmax/2. The intersection of this line with the x and y profiles sets the major and minor radii of the ellipse approximating the shape of the vortex, also shown as the red ellipse in the main graph. Using the ratio between these radii, the anisotropy of the vortex, AB, is calculated, and is shown on the plot.

FIG. 4. The anisotropy of the magnetic field in the vortex core AB with α = −1 as a function of F4 and the strain ϵ. (a) and (c) are in the nematic phase with β = 0.1, while (b) and (d) are in the quasi-chiral phase with β = −0.1. The anisotropy changes parametrically slower for the quasi-chiral case, as O(|ϵF4|), while it changes as O(|F4|) in the nematic case. Changing from F2 = 0 in (a) and (b) to F2 = 0.5 in (c) and (d) retains the scaling, but the anisotropy of the vortex decreases with increasing F2.

FIG. 6. Ratio between the low temperature anisotropy of the magnetic field in the vortex core, AB with α = −1, and the anisotropy of the critical field, AHc2, near the transition (which, by Eq. (14) and Ref. 24, is independent of α for −2|ϵ/F4| < α < |ϵ|) as a function of F4 and the strain ϵ. (a) and (c) are in the nematic phase with β = 0.1, while (b) and (d) are in the quasi-chiral phase with β = −0.1. A clear variation of the anisotropy ratio under change of ϵ is seen in the quasi-chiral phase while it is nearly constant in the nematic phase. Changing from F2 = 0 in (a) and (b) to F2 = 0.5 in (c) and (d) retains the scaling but the anisotropy of the vortex decreases with increasing F2.
